title: Baillie–PSW pseudoprimes
formal: Does there exist a composite integer n that passes the strong base-2 probable-prime test and the strong Lucas probable-prime test with Selfridge’s Method A, including the parameter-search rejection rule specified below?
why: Tests the mathematical reliability of a widely used primality-testing combination.

progress.text: The Fermat/Lucas combination originates in the work recounted by Baillie, Fiori and Wagstaff.
The paper records verification below \(2^{64}\), proves Method \(A/A\)* equivalences and proposes additional checks.
A selected-composite experiment reports no strong-Lucas survivors and does not resolve the universal question.

definitions: A composite integer is an integer \(n>1\) with a divisor strictly between 1 and n. Even integers greater than 2 and perfect squares are rejected; thus a candidate here is odd and nonsquare. Write \(n- 1=2^{s} d\) with d odd. The strong base-2 test accepts if \(2^{d}\equiv 1\) (mod n), or \(2^{2^{r} d}\equiv - 1\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<s\). For the Lucas test, examine \(D=5,- 7,9,- 11,13,- 15,\ldots\) in that order, namely \(D_{k}=(- 1)^{k}(2k+5)\) for \(k\ge 0\). At each step reject if \(1<\gcd (|D|,n)<n\); otherwise stop at the first D with Jacobi symbol \((D/n)=- 1\). For odd \(n=\prod p_{j}^{e_{j}}\), the Jacobi symbol \((a/n)\) is \(\prod (a/p_{j})^{e}_{j}\), where \((a/p)\) is 0 if p divides a, +1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and −1 otherwise. This defines the symbol without requiring factorization as an implementation. Squares were excluded because their Jacobi symbols cannot be −1; for odd nonsquares the search terminates. Set \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). Define integer sequences \(U_{0}=0, U_{1}=1, V_{0}=2, V_{1}=\mathrm{P}\) and, for \(j\ge 0, U_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} U_{j+1}- Q U_{j}\) and \(V_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} V_{j+1}- Q V_{j}\). Write \(n+1=2^{t} u\) with u odd. The strong Lucas test accepts if \(U_{u}\equiv 0\) (mod n), or \(V_{2^{r} u}\equiv 0\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<t\). Passing means surviving the parameter search and satisfying both strong tests, with exact integer congruences. The number 2 is accepted separately but cannot answer this composite-existence question. No extra trial-division cutoff, random bases or additional congruence checks are part of the specified variant.
answer_criterion: Give a composite n together with a proof of compositeness and exact verification of the parameter search and both acceptance conditions, or prove that no composite integer passes this specified variant. A finite search bound, a heuristic count of expected counterexamples or a counterexample to only one component does not settle the question.

context_blocks.title: Why combine two tests
context_blocks.text: A composite can imitate some arithmetic properties of primes. For example, \(2047=23\cdot 89\) passes the strong base-2 test because \(2^{1023}\equiv 1\) modulo 2047. It fails the strong Lucas test with \(D=5\). The question is whether a composite can evade both parts together, however large it is.

context_blocks.title: The exact variant matters
context_blocks.text: Selfridge’s Method A fixes \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). The main source also describes Method A*, which changes P and Q to 5 when \(D=5\), and proves equivalence of the strong Lucas outcomes for integers coprime to 10. Its proposed strengthened test adds further congruences. This card keeps the imported strong base-2 plus strong Lucas target and spells out Method A.

context_blocks.title: What exhaustive computation establishes
context_blocks.text: The 2021 paper reports that no base-2 Fermat pseudoprime below \(2^{64}\) also passes its Lucas test, giving correctness through that finite range and hence ruling out smaller counterexamples to the strong combination. It reports no known larger counterexample. Such a bound leaves the existence question over all integers unanswered.

context_blocks.title: Recent evidence has finite scope
context_blocks.text: A January 2026 preprint reports that all 200 selected composites in its experiment fail the strong Lucas test despite passing several Miller–Rabin bases. This does not establish correctness for arbitrary integers or a rigorous independence theorem for the two tests. With the specified parameters, the test’s outcome on a fixed n is deterministic; “probable prime” describes the strength of the conclusion, not random choices made here.

sentences: The Baillie–PSW combination checks a prime-like modular power pattern and a prime-like Lucas sequence pattern.
The question asks whether any composite integer passes both strong tests with the specified Selfridge parameters.
All recurrences, congruences and parameter-search rejection rules are fixed in the statement.
Exhaustive verification through a large finite range and later experiments have produced no counterexample in the checked sources.
A single rigorously verified composite would answer yes, while answering no requires a proof covering integers of every size.
